claims.text: A refractory HEA formulated primarily from W, Nb, Mo, and Ta can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed alloy is in an as-cast state.
The proposed alloy has a multiphase microstructure.
The proposed alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed alloy has an intended low-activation elemental makeup.
The proposed test intervention is exposure to high temperature and high neutron flux representative of fusion plasma operations.
The relevant simulated environment includes high thermal loads and neutron irradiation.
The alloy develops or maintains a stabilized multi-element solid-solution microstructure.
The stabilized multi-element solid solution promotes sluggish diffusion.
The stabilized multi-element solid solution provides effective defect trapping.
High-melting-point refractory elements in the HEA matrix enhance mechanical stability.
Reduced defect mobility enhances irradiation resistance.
Careful elemental selection minimizes the production of long-lived radioactive isotopes.
The alloy will retain high-temperature mechanical performance under fusion-relevant conditions.
The alloy will exhibit lower induced radioactivity than conventional plasma-facing materials.
The beneficial effects are anticipated at operating temperatures below approximately 2000 degrees Celsius.
Performance may deviate when temperature or neutron exposure exceeds the proposed operational limits.
Precise activation levels remain to be quantitatively determined experimentally.
Long-term microstructural evolution under extended irradiation remains to be quantitatively determined experimentally.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described simultaneously as multiphase and as a single-phase solid solution, without explaining whether these refer to different scales, regions, or processing stages.
